newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian cement giant to see sharp fall in 96/97 net.
newsitem.headline: Indian cement giant to see sharp fall in 96/97 net.

text.p: Spiralling input costs and an oversupply in major markets will drag the net of India's largest cement maker Associated Cement Companies (ACC) sharply lower in the year ended March, analysts said on Tuesday.

"Volumes were flat during the year. On the other hand the company was faced with falling realisations and the rising cost of inputs like coal and power," said Jitendra Sriram, cement analyst at HSBC B&K Securities.
"Freight rates also went up by 10 percent," he added. ACC transports more than 14 million tonnes of cement and inputs such as coal each year.
The company is due to release its 1996/97 (April-March) results on Wednesday. Analysts from 28 securities houses polled by Reuters in April had forecast an average net profit of 951 million rupees.
ACC said earlier this year cement sales -- including sales of purchased cement and exports -- totalled around 9.8 million tonnes, from 9.4 million tonnes in 1995/96.
"Cement demand was sluggish in most of the markets, particularly in the second half of the year," ACC said.
Sriram said he expected a net of 830 million, down sharply from 2.27 billion rupees in 1995/96.
Worse than expected first half results announced by the firm in November had stunned analysts and many reiterated a bearish outlook on the industry, which has been hit by oversupply and slack demand.
ACC's net profit tumbled 56 percent to 550.5 million rupees in the six months to September 30, 1996. Most analysts had been expecting a first half net of around 800-900 million rupees.
"The company could not recover from an unprecedented increase in the cost of inputs that were beyond the company's control," ACC said in its first half results statement.

ACC shares plummetted in the run-up to the first half results but have remained steady at around 1,100 rupees to 1,200 rupees since November. The firm's shares were trading 56 rupees higher at 1,205 on the Bombay bourse on Tuesday.
Analysts said a fall in cement prices due to an oversupply in northern and eastern India -- where ACC sells more than 40 percent of its output -- had hit the company during the year.
"ACC had a tough time during the last quarter of calendar 1996 when cement prices fell in all markets except probably in the south," said Pradeep Mahtani, analyst at Jardine Fleming India Broking.
"Average prices in the second half of 1996/97 were lower than in the first half of the year," Mahtani said.
Analyst Dhawal Mehta at UBS Securities said cement companies would continue to be plagued by problems of oversupply during the current 1997/98 financial year.
"1997/98 is going to be another bad year for cement. Costs have gone up across the board again this year -- I don't see an improvement," Mehta said.

"Capacities have gone up substantially over the last couple of years. There's too much cement coming into the market and there's no way this can be absorbed though demand is growing at around 7.0 to 8.0 percent annually," he added.
